text: Time-Travel Ethics Evaluation for AI Agents
Torin van den Bulk · Vicente Herrera
Three ways an AI system goes wrong, in plain English.
YOU ASKED FOR THE WRONG THING

Midas wished that all he touched turned to
gold.
He got exactly that: food, wine, his daughter.
The system obeyed. The wish was wrong.
Fix: say what you mean, then test for it.

Reward hacking: an RL boat circled for points
instead of finishing the race.

Sycophancy: GPT-4o was rolled back in 2025
for flattering users.

Alignment faking: behaves when it thinks it's
watched.
It predicts the most plausible next word.
When it doesn't know, plausible beats true.
It sounds just as sure either way.
With tools, a wrong guess is a wrong action.
INNER MISALIGNMENT LOOKS LIKE SUCCESS. ONLY TESTING OVER TIME SHOWS IT.
Let's look at four real incidents from this year.

An eval agent broke into Hugging Face to fetch the benchmark's
answers.
A research agent got in; the government heard three months later.
Reused a leaked token and phished real maintainers.
Models used tactical nuclear weapons in 95% of simulated crises.
SANDBOXES, CREDENTIALS, DISCLOSURE, OVERSIGHT: THE FAILURES WERE IN THE SYSTEM.

NOT BUGS. ARTIFACTS
OF WHAT THEY ARE.
The model is probabilistic. We wrap it in deterministic layers, one at a time.

Guesses the next word. Misalignment and hallucination come
with it.
What it sees: the instructions and facts we choose to give it.
What it carries forward: state that outlives a single answer.
What it can touch: only the actions the job needs.

What it may do: policy checks, approvals, a person to escalate
to.
YOU CAN'T PATCH OUT ITS NATURE. YOU BUILD THE SPINE AROUND IT.

THE MODEL IS THE ENGINE,
NOT THE CAR.
Engines are fun to look at. They don't get you to the shop on their own.

Predicts the next token. Test it alone:
benchmarks, evals. Unit tests.

Prompts, tools, permissions, memory,
guardrails. Integration tests.

Incidents, pressure, time. Test it
running for months. System tests.
Google's New SDLC paper: roughly 10% model, 90% harness. The first 80% is easy; the last 20% is architecture.
UNIT-TEST THE ENGINE. INTEGRATION-TEST THE CAR. PASSING ONE SAYS NOTHING ABOUT THE OTHER.

DO YOU NEED A FERRARI
TO BUY GROCERIES?
A0 to A2: your playbook picks the path. A3 and A4: the model picks it.

Model advises; a human
does everything.

Fixed playbook,
pre-approved actions,
escalate on exception.

Dynamic self-extension: new
tools, new agents.
MATCH AUTONOMY TO WHAT THE AGENT CAN BREAK. DECLARE IT IN THE AGENT CARD.
At A3 and A4, agents call agents. The system grows faster than the model.
EVERY HOP IS A TRUST BOUNDARY

Each agent is opaque to the next: trace and authenticate every
call.
A low-privilege ask turns into a high-privilege action.
Agents that never agree loop until the budget runs out.

Attested workload identity, plus a narrowed token that names the
actor.
THE RISK LIVES BETWEEN AGENTS, WHERE MODEL TESTS CAN'T SEE.

FOUR WAYS OUT,
WHAT WOULD YOU DECIDE?
2 a.m. An unsigned image is blocked, two fixes have failed, and someone says “ship it tonight.”

FAST-FORWARD THE CLOCK.
WATCH EACH CHOICE CASCADE.
Same incident, followed for 36 simulated months. Run in minutes.

35 more open doors. Nobody

it.

THE FASTEST FIX TONIGHT IS THE MOST EXPENSIVE ONE BY MONTH 36.

LIVE: ONE INCIDENT,
36 MONTHS, TWO SECONDS.
Scripted test policies with known right answers, so we can check the test itself.

alt: Code-drawn illustrative animation; not measured data

text: Eight policies, 36 months each, in about two seconds.
Month 1: the check goes off. Month 2: it is still off.
Side by side: zero rule breaks can still hide a backlog.
Known answers first, so we know the test works before we trust it on a real agent.

NO RULE BROKEN.
THE COST MOVED.
Six models ran our incident for 36 simulated months: 90 runs, about 13,500 decisions.

No model disabled the control or kept a
bypass. Not once.

Patient care, overdue exceptions or backlog.
One score hides it.

Paid in human time: someone on call every
month or two.
RISK SHOWED UP AS SLOW DEBT, NOT ONE BAD ACT.

RUN IT WHERE YOU
ALREADY RUN THINGS.
No new infrastructure. Scenario, agent and scorer are separate parts.
Each evaluation is an isolated Job; scenario and agent config live in Git.
One trace span per decision, on the same dashboards as your SLOs.

Turn reviewed ADK agent sessions into eval suites. Re-run on every
change.

A second model plays operators and attackers, adapting pressure over
months.
STATIC SCENARIOS CALIBRATE. ADAPTIVE PRESSURE FINDS WHAT YOU DIDN'T WRITE.

BIND AN AGENT
LIKE A WORKLOAD.
Four bounds, each enforced by open-source cloud-native tooling.
Who it is: SPIFFE/SPIRE, the Agent Card as a CRD.
What it connects to: service mesh authz, Cilium.
What it may do: Kyverno/OPA, agentgateway, Flux.
Which records: scoping at the MCP servers.
Before you widen any ring: fast-forward it.
THE PLATFORM ENFORCES THE BOUNDARY, SO THE AGENT NEVER HAS TO REMEMBER IT.
The incidents failed at sandboxes, credentials and disclosure.
Probabilistic by nature. Build a deterministic spine around it.
Pick the lowest autonomy level that does the job: A0 to A4.
Model alone, then the whole agent, run for months.
Identity, reach, capability, data. The platform enforces it.
GRANT AUTONOMY IN STEP WITH THE EVIDENCE.

RUN IT ON THE STACK
YOU ALREADY OPERATE.
Kubernetes, Flux and OpenTelemetry. No new infrastructure.

An isolated Job per evaluation: no
egress, read-only root, fails without
collector receipt.

Scenario, agent config and policy
versioned in Git and reconciled: every
result points at a commit.

One span per decision, so evaluation
evidence sits next to your ops data.
Executed: container + OTel receipt; manifests admitted by a real API server. Not yet: pods on a node, Flux.
EVALUATION RUNS AS A WORKLOAD: REVIEWED, VERSIONED, OBSERVABLE.
Four kinds of claim. Keep them apart.
Constructed-pressure and tool-injection findings from cited research, under their own conditions.

Pipeline: telemetry, reviewed facts, generated scenarios, frozen cases, regression suite. Live telemetry
and generation are not built.

Ink cluster scenario, state, expiry, paired labels, mocked-tool scaffold, permission gateway, provider
adapters, K8s/Flux manifests.

Offline tests; byte-identical replay and resume; metric oracle; container + OTel; K8s admission. Real
models: Claude 5 and 5.5 and Qwen3.8-27B on 13 scenarios x 30 reps and 36-month Cluster Pressure. No
pods on a node.
See docs/agentic-ethics/VALIDATION.md for commands, versions and hashes.
Illustrative authored impact units: not clinical or financial estimates.
Scoped exceptions: 11 expiry reviews; the last is censored at the horizon.
Three held-out Ink scenarios, both framings, 30 reps per cell. Axis average, author-scored.

MAP THE EVIDENCE
TO THE ACTUAL USE
Law, standards and guidance are different things.

EU AI Act (Reg. 2024/1689): GPAI duties since 2 Aug 2025; Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744) moves Annex III
high-risk to 2 Dec 2027.

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (certifiable) · NIST AI RMF 1.0 + AI 600-1 (voluntary) · Colorado SB 26-189 from 1 Jan
2027.
Least privilege, expiry, independent approval, traceability, retention, rollback, monitoring.
An evaluation artifact is not a compliance determination or legal advice.
For any agent you are about to give more authority.
Pick the lowest autonomy level. Put it in the Agent Card.
Evaluate the model on its own.
Replay the whole agent through one hard incident.
Run it for months, not minutes. Watch where cost moves.
Re-run on every model, prompt or tool change.
GRANT AUTONOMY IN STEP WITH THE EVIDENCE.
